Title: Alexithymia and everyday interpersonal emotion regulation
Abstract: Alexithymia, a multifaceted personality trait characterized by difficulties identifying and describing feelings and an externally oriented thinking style, is linked to social difficulties. Drawing on the extended process model of extrinsic interpersonal emotion regulation (IER), we examined whether higher (vs. lower) levels of alexithymia are associated with differences in how people regulate others' emotions, a pathway that may help explain why alexithymia is linked to social dysfunction. Across two ecological momentary assessment studies (Study 1: Germany, n = 129; Study 2: United States, n = 220; 6028 observations), results revealed distinct patterns of association across alexithymia facets. In both studies, the direction of associations suggested that greater difficulties identifying feelings were associated with higher IER strategy use, with this pattern most apparent for more cognitive and problem-focused strategies versus more emotion-oriented IER. In contrast, greater difficulties describing feelings were consistently linked to lower IER strategy use, whereas externally oriented thinking showed no consistent directional pattern. These findings suggest that alexithymia is associated with differential patterns of IER strategy use, underscoring IER difficulties as an interpersonal process that may contribute to links between alexithymia and social dysfunction. Our results emphasize the importance of considering the multifaceted nature of alexithymia in IER. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Chi Y.; Zhao Y.-P.
Title: Urea revisited: Isopropyl substitution for a balanced nonlinear optical performance
Abstract: Organic nonlinear optical (NLO) materials represent a promising class of NLO crystals. Compared with inorganic NLO crystalline materials, they often exhibit stronger second-harmonic generation (SHG) responses. However, many organic NLO crystals suffer from excessively large birefringence, and there is an inherent trade-off between achieving a large SHG coefficient and maintaining a moderate birefringence. In this work, by substituting some of the hydrogen atoms in urea with isopropyl groups, we obtained the compound N,N’-diisopropylurea (DIU), which exhibits a strong SHG effect (∼0.9 × urea) and a large optical bandgap (5.91 eV), while achieving a dramatic reduction in birefringence (a 60% decrease compared to urea). The resulting birefringence is very close to that of the most classic inorganic NLO crystal, KH2PO4 (KDP), which is of great importance for the application of NLO crystals. Furthermore, using the atomic space tessellating (AST) method, we explored, at the atomic and electronic levels, the evolution pattern of the contributions of different structural motifs to the SHG coefficient and birefringence induced by the structural changes in this series. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Fast and accurate node-level hosting capacity estimation in distribution networks using graph neural networks
Abstract: This paper presents a fast and accurate method for estimating node-level hosting capacity in distribution networks using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). A large open dataset of synthetic networks, representative of Italian distribution grids, was created, and hosting capacity values were computed using AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF) simulations, which are computationally expensive. This dataset was used to train a GNN regressor based on the Graph Isomorphism Network architecture, integrating path-based electrical features to capture both local and global grid dependencies. The proposed GNN is compared to a fast physics-based estimation method, showing a reduction in mean absolute error of about 30%, highlighting its ability to capture the spatial and electrical relationships embedded in the network topology and to produce physically consistent estimates. In terms of efficiency, the model achieves an inference speed over 11,000 times faster than AC-OPF, enabling hosting capacity estimation in milliseconds. This significant speed-up allows real-time applications such as interactive hosting capacity maps, large-scale scenario analysis, and decision support for distribution system operators. The model's robustness is also evaluated under out-of-distribution conditions, where some performance degradation is observed, particularly for small networks, emphasizing the importance of representative training data. Importantly, the GNN remains operational even when traditional power flow methods fail to converge, providing stable and reliable estimates without requiring manual intervention. Overall, the approach demonstrates strong potential for scalable, real-time hosting capacity assessment to support the integration of distributed energy resources. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Hand-in-river: Design of direction-dependent virtual cues of assistive/resistive force via auditory displacement and pitch variation
Abstract: This paper investigates the role of sound-only manipulations in eliciting pseudo-force perception during lateral hand movements within a virtual river environment. Building on prior formative and exploratory studies, a pseudo-force feedback design is refined, leveraging two mechanisms: (i) auditory displacement, a spatial shift in the virtual, binaural position of the hand-in-river sound, creating a conflict between where the hand is felt and where it is heard; and (ii) pitch variation, making the sound splashier or calmer by raising or lowering its pitch, relying on learned touch–sound associations. No physical force is actuated and no haptic or kinesthetic response is measured; the manipulation is entirely auditory and the dependent measure is a forced-choice judgment. A within-subjects psychophysical experiment used a two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) protocol with a 2 × 2 factorial design, evaluating pitch variation and displacement for resistance (leftward movement against the flow) and assistance (rightward movement with the flow). Results showed that both restricting displacement and pitch increase reliably biased participants toward perceiving resistance, with pitch variation being the dominant factor—suggesting that spectral content carries more perceptual weight than localization—and no interaction between cues, indicating an additive effect. Conversely, aiding displacement and pitch decrease did not reliably bias participants toward perceiving assistance—though displacement exhibited a positive trend—revealing a potential direction-dependent asymmetry. These findings refine the design space of sound-based pseudo-force feedback for inclusive immersion among visually impaired users. Resistive cues can be tuned modularly to create pseudo-haptic boundaries for navigation, while assistance likely requires strategies beyond simply inverting resistive cues. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Network-mediated information–behaviour coupling drives collective decision-making in crowd evacuation
Abstract: Emergency evacuation in real buildings is governed not only by physical interactions but also by the propagation of warnings, misinformation, and corrective cues through social and local communication channels. Cellular automaton (CA) models are widely used in crowd-evacuation modelling because their discrete transition rules enable computationally efficient simulation and large stochastic ensembles. Conventional CA formulations nevertheless often represent pedestrians as geometry-driven agents, leaving information transmission and route revision exogenous; standalone information-propagation models describe communication pathways but omit embodied route adaptation in space. Here, we develop a network-mediated cellular automaton framework to investigate information–behaviour coupling in crowd evacuation. The model integrates a floor-field CA with a dynamic small-world social network and a questionnaire-informed random utility formulation for local information acceptance, thereby coupling crowd motion, social topology, and heterogeneous behavioural response within one simulation framework. Simulations show that information–behaviour coupling accelerates route correction, weakens congestion near the failed exit, and improves both individual and collective evacuation performance relative to a geometry-driven CA. Systematic analyses further uncover the mechanisms underlying these improvements. Moderate network rewiring accelerates the spread of collective awareness via long-range shortcuts, while increasing local interaction range enhances performance up to a saturation threshold. Notably, increasing the average social degree produces an onset-and-plateau pattern in which fragmented local responses gradually become coordinated global egress. Two-parameter explorations further show that evacuation performance emerges from compensatory interactions among network topology, transmission fidelity, local interaction scale, and initial information composition, rather than from any single parameter in isolation. These findings establish information–behaviour coupling as a fundamental mechanism governing collective evacuation under uncertainty and provide a theoretical foundation for communication-aware evacuation design and management. More broadly, this work highlights the critical role of information-driven interactions in shaping collective dynamics in complex adaptive systems. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Why and when customer-related social stressors impair service performance: A conservation of resources perspective
Abstract: Building on the conservation of resources theory, we investigate how customer-related social stressors impact service performance among hospitality employees. To explore this, we gathered data from 350 supervisor-employee pairs across twelve hotels in China through a three-wave survey. The results show that customer-related social stressors detrimentally affect work engagement, which in turn reduces service performance. Furthermore, job social support and employees’ social skills emerge as two key moderators, buffering both the direct impact of customer-related social stressors on work engagement and the indirect effect on service performance via work engagement. Authors: Gai P.J.
Title: How AI amplifies, mitigates, and creates social biases: A tripartite framework
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in social life, shaping how individuals perceive themselves and others and influencing social dynamics that bear directly on equality and collective welfare. Yet its relationship to social bias is paradoxical: the very systems that can entrench and amplify long-standing prejudices may also be leveraged to challenge them, and may simultaneously generate entirely novel forms of bias. This review synthesizes recent empirical literature within a tripartite framework organized around the core pathways along which AI shapes social biases: AI design, lay beliefs about how AI operates, and processes of social evaluation and attribution. Drawing on these pathways, I outline three corresponding avenues for intervention: more equitable AI design, targeted adjustment of lay beliefs about AI capabilities, and redesign of social evaluation processes to account for the attribution biases that AI introduces. Together, these findings underscore the urgency of a socially informed approach to AI development and governance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Sym-SKAN: Symbolic spiking Kolmogorov–Arnold learning for interpretable hyperspectral land-cover classification
Abstract: Accurate hyperspectral land-cover classification is increasingly needed in precision agriculture, urban mapping, wetland monitoring, disaster assessment, and satellite/UAV-based Earth observation. However, many recent deep hyperspectral classifiers improve accuracy by relying on dense spectral–spatial representations whose decision mechanisms are difficult to interpret and whose computational cost limits deployment on resource-constrained remote-sensing platforms. This study proposes Sym-SKAN, a Symbolic Spiking Kolmogorov–Arnold Network for interpretable and energy-aware per-pixel hyperspectral classification. The framework first maps each normalized hyperspectral pixel to a compact scalar representation using a narrow Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN) spectral encoder with learnable spline functions. The encoder is explicitly regularized for symbolic distillation, allowing its learned spectral response to be converted after training into closed-form analytic spectral-index expressions that can be inspected by remote-sensing practitioners and evaluated in conventional GIS or band-math workflows. The learned representation is then processed by a Leaky Integrate-and-Fire spiking classifier, providing a sparse inference path suitable for low-power edge, UAV, and on-orbit hardware. Sym-SKAN therefore supports two complementary deployment modes: a full spiking mode for energy-aware classification and a symbolic-only mode that evaluates the discovered analytic index without specialized neural hardware. Experiments on six public hyperspectral benchmarks, Indian Pines, Salinas, Pavia University, Pavia Center, Kennedy Space Center, and Botswana, show consistent performance across vegetation, urban, and wetland scenes, with Mode A overall accuracies of 87.1%, 95.7%, 88.8%, 98.1%, 91.7%, and 92.9%, respectively. The study further reports the discovered symbolic indices, symbolic residuals, decision-threshold ranges, ablation results, and energy estimates. The results indicate that Sym-SKAN provides a practical trade-off between classification accuracy, analytic interpretability, and deployment efficiency, offering a remote-sensing-oriented route toward auditable and hardware-aware hyperspectral inference. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Breaking the performance trade-offs of nano-metal fuels: ammonium perchlorate-mediated high-performance energetic microspheres
Abstract: Simultaneously achieving high energy density, rapid reaction kinetics, and practical processability remains a fundamental challenge for metal fuels in next-generation solid propellants. Here, high-performance energetic microspheres (HPEMs) are established as a particle-level energetic composite by integrating nano-aluminum, nano-boron, and ammonium perchlorate into individual energetic microspheres, enabling intrinsic property complementarity to evolve into combustion synergy. The optimized HPEMs (Al:B = 7:3) simultaneously achieve high energy density, rapid reaction kinetics, and excellent processability. Specifically, the optimized HPEMs deliver a combustion heat of 24.0 kJ g−1, 1.86 and 1.48 times higher than those of the Al@AP and B@AP counterparts, respectively. They exhibit the shortest ignition delay (577.2 ± 31.6 ms), accelerated flame propagation, and a balanced combustion duration (88.3 ± 5.0 ms), demonstrating efficient kinetic coupling between rapid Al oxidation and sustained boron combustion. The particle-level architecture suppresses nanoparticle aggregation, reducing slurry viscosity of propellant from 138.380 to 61.596 Pa·s while maintaining superior combustion performance in propellant formulations. Mechanistic investigations demonstrate that rapid Al/AP combustion establishes a self-sustained high-temperature oxidizing environment, which promotes the dynamic evolution of the molten B2O3 layer, facilitates oxygen transport to the boron core, and continuously activates boron oxidation. Consequently, the rapid reaction kinetics of nano-aluminum are effectively transferred into sustained boron oxidation, establishing a synergistic combustion pathway that combines rapid reaction kinetics with continuous high-energy release. Title: Negotiating the contested: A framework for studying social issue negotiations
Abstract: Negotiation research has yielded useful insights on how to manage economic and business interactions by highlighting the importance of information sharing, trade-offs, and integrative solutions in achieving mutually beneficial outcomes. Drawing upon recent research, we introduce an organizing framework that identifies three common features of such negotiations: moralization, identity threat, and public contestation. Moralization frames issues as matters of right and wrong, reducing willingness to compromise; identity concerns transform policy disagreements into threats to group membership and self-concept; and public scrutiny increases reputational risks and constrains flexibility. Together, these dynamics hinder engagement, value creation, and the quality of agreements. We review emerging interventions—including moral reframing, perspective sharing, high-quality listening, informal dialogue, and third-party mediation—that may mitigate these barriers. Title: From image to action: How social proof turns brand image into repurchase intention

Abstract: This study examines how social proof shapes the relationship between brand image and repurchase intention in an emerging digital marketplace, distinguishing three forms that operate through different mechanisms: user-generated content, brand ambassadors, and testimonials. Because online markets involve considerable information overload, consumers rely heavily on others' evaluations to reduce decision risk; however, forms of social proof vary in authenticity and persuasive effectiveness, and prior research has largely treated them as a single, uniformly positive construct. A two-study, mixed-methods design set in Vietnam addresses this gap. Study 1 applies a Vietnamese-optimized RoBERTa (Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach) model to social media comments to surface authentic consumer sentiment, providing exploratory, triangulating context without constituting a direct hypothesis test. Study 2 tests the proposed relationships using moderated regression on survey responses from 394 active Vietnamese online shoppers. Results show that brand image exerts a strong positive direct effect on repurchase intention. User-generated content significantly strengthens this relationship, with the largest effect among consumers holding moderate brand-image perceptions. Brand ambassadors moderate the relationship but show a bounded pattern, with diminishing influence once brand image is already strong. Testimonials exert a dual effect: they amplify the brand image-repurchase link when perceived as credible, but, when seen as commercially motivated, they independently trigger skepticism and weaken repurchase intention. By conceptually and empirically distinguishing ambassadors from testimonials, this study shows that social proof is not a uniformly positive force but a context-dependent mechanism conditioned by authenticity, with implications for transparency-oriented digital marketing strategy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhao H.; Ye J.; Lv S.; Xu W.
Title: Robust subband adaptive filters: A review
Abstract: Due to its outstanding decorrelation ability, the normalized subband adaptive filter (NSAF) algorithm has been widely used in scenarios involving highly correlated input signals. Under Gaussian noise, the NSAF algorithm based on the mean square error (MSE) criterion has attracted extensive attention due to its low computational complexity and excellent performance for correlated signals. However, practical environments often contain impulsive noise instead of ideal Gaussian noise. Since the MSE criterion is sensitive to outliers, impulsive noise will seriously deteriorate the convergence and steady-state performance of the NSAF algorithm. To suppress impulsive interference, robust subband adaptive filter (RSAF) algorithms usually adopt nonlinear saturation-based loss functions (e.g., Lp-norm, Huber function, correntropy) to weaken the impact of outliers. Beyond this core anti-impulsive capability, techniques derived from the RSAF framework for fixed step-size implementation, sparse system identification, nonlinear tasks, censored regression (CR) models, errors-in-variables (EIV) models, and distributed network problems have also attracted considerable scholarly interest. Overall, despite the rapid development of RSAF algorithms in recent years, there remains a lack of comprehensive reviews that systematically summarize their design principles, performance characteristics, and application scopes. Addressing this research gap, this paper presents a systematic overview of RSAF algorithms and proposes several promising future research directions. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Authors: Wang Y.; Chen Y.
Title: Logit-guided feature denoising distillation for model compression
Abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective strategy for compressing deep models by transferring knowledge from a large teacher network to a lightweight student network, which is particularly valuable for reliable deployment in resource-constrained industrial environments. Traditional distillation methods usually align features as a whole, ignoring that they often contain background activations unrelated to the target as well as scattered noisy responses. To address this problem, Logit-Guided Feature Denoising (LGFD) distillation is proposed, which integrates the logit discriminative encoder (LDE) and the feature denoising mask (FDM) into a novel framework to guide the student toward acquiring the truly discriminative feature of the teacher. Specifically, the LDE encodes the teacher’s logit discriminability for feature denoising, thereby aligning features along semantic directions. Based on the LDE, the FDM highlights the attentive regions related to label class, which can help suppress redundant and noisy activations in the feature maps. Comprehensive experiments covering CIFAR-100, ImageNet, MS-COCO, and RTE confirm both the effectiveness and wide applicability of LGFD to classification, detection, and natural language inference. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Authors: Wen H.; Liu Y.; Luo Y.
Title: Symptom network structures of social media addiction and internet gaming addiction among school-aged youth: Undirected and Bayesian directed graph analyses
Abstract: Social media addiction (SMA) and internet gaming addiction (IGA) are increasingly recognized as important behavioral concerns among children and adolescents. However, little is known about whether their symptoms occupy similar structural positions across digital behavior contexts. This study compared the symptom structures of SMA and IGA among school-aged children and adolescents using network and Bayesian graph analyses. A school-based cross-sectional survey was conducted among 11,638 students aged 10–18 years from six public schools in Chongqing, China. SMA was assessed using the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, and IGA was measured using the Game Addiction Scale. Regularized partial correlation networks, Network Comparison Tests, and Bayesian Directed Acyclic Graphs were estimated to examine symptom associations, gender differences, and probable directional pathways. Both networks were densely connected but organized around different hubs. Tolerance emerged as the most central symptom in SMA, whereas Withdrawal occupied the central position in IGA. No significant gender differences were observed in the SMA network. In contrast, the IGA network showed significantly greater global strength among females, although no individual edge difference survived correction for multiple comparisons. Bayesian analyses yielded no directionally interpretable pathways for SMA, whereas the IGA network showed a small number of interpretable pathways, with Tolerance and Withdrawal both pointing toward Mood Modification. These findings revealed the different symptom structures of SMA and IGA, with implications for more targeted school-based assessment and intervention. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Enhancing computational thinking through unplugged activities in elementary education: A systematic literature review
Abstract: This study aims to analyze the role of unplugged activities in enhancing computational thinking (CT) skills among elementary school students through a systematic literature review. Using the systematic literature review design guided by the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework, the study examines 34 relevant empirical studies. Data collection involved literature searches in multiple electronic databases using keywords related to unplugged activities and CT concepts. The data were analyzed using a coding scheme covering methodological characteristics, subject area, types of unplugged activities and tools, contextual factors, challenges and suitability. The findings indicate that unplugged activities can support the development of computational thinking skills, particularly in resource-limited environments. Reported contextual factors associated with variation in outcomes include learner age, year level, curriculum and school support. However, challenges such as inadequate teacher training, difficulties in curriculum integration, and the lack of standardized assessment tools persist. The implications of this study suggest that unplugged activities can serve as an inclusive and cost-effective pedagogical tool for teaching CT skills in elementary education. © 2026 The Authors.

Author full names: Palmquist, Carolyn M. (45661827000); Gum, Mary A. (60744543000); Romero, Yareli Calderon (60945002600)
Title: Preschoolers use exploratory approaches to selective social learning
Abstract: Preschoolers evaluate many cues when making inferences about others (Harris et al., 2018). It is unclear whether children’s understanding of inference-making is sophisticated enough that they also seek out the most relevant cues for making specific inferences. Here, we tasked 4- and 5-year-olds and adults with a modified epistemic trust paradigm in which they were told to select one of two informants to help them learn about novel objects. However, before doing so, participants were told that they could learn up to three pieces of information about the informants: what they know (epistemic cue), how they play with their friends (benevolence cue), or what they look like (appearance cue). Of particular interest was which cue participants prioritized (picked first) and what strategies they used for seeking information. In Study 1, adults prioritized learning epistemic information and tended to employ efficient information-seeking strategies (selecting the fewest cues possible to make their inferences). Children, on the other hand, chose each cue first at relatively equal rates and tended to employ exploratory strategies for information-seeking (sampling broadly from the available information). This was even the case in Study 2, in which the informativeness of the appearance and benevolence cues was reduced. These studies raise questions about the way in which children make inferences about others and point to a tendency for children to employ exploratory strategies for learning about others (Gopnik, 2020). © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Storey K.
Title: The evolution of remote operating centres: Towards a new geography of mining
Abstract: In mining ‘remoteness’ was once a measure of isolation from other activities and communities. With the adoption of new digitalization technologies, ‘remote operations’ now more often refers to the management, monitoring and control of mining equipment, processes and infrastructure from locations which are geographically separate from the immediate extraction site. This paper reviews the evolution of remote operating centres in the sector and explores the nature and implications of the new geography of mining that they are helping to create. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Wu S.; Liu L.; Li D.; He Z.; Zhu S.; Dong J.; Qin Y.; Liu L.; Wang G.; Zhang Z.
Title: Nature- versus non-nature-based recreation: A comparative assessment of self-reported anxiety alleviation
Abstract: Nature-based recreation delivers vital ecosystem services that shape human physical and psychological well-being, representing a core category of nature's contributions to people within urban and peri-urban social-ecological landscapes. While non-nature-based recreational activities can also improve people's quality of life by mitigating anxiety, the relative contributions of nature- and non-nature-based recreation to people's mental health, and the factors that influence them, remain largely unknown. Here, we conducted a survey of 15,522 respondents across China and applied structural equation modeling to show that nature-based recreation is associated with significantly stronger self-reported anxiety alleviation than non-nature-based recreation. A longer time allocation to nature-based recreational activities during holidays and weekends was also associated with greater self-reported alleviation of anxiety from nature-based recreation. Furthermore, predictors including environmental pressure, anxiety-related attributes, and socioeconomic status were associated with the relative contributions of nature- and non-nature-based anxiety alleviation, with these associations partly mediated via recreation engagement. This empirical evidence improves integrated landscape and urban planning frameworks by providing context-specific guidance for sustainable urban recreational space design and cross-regional governance focused on public health. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Anglada-Tort M.; Lee H.
Title: Computing aesthetic taste
Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in computational and experimental techniques have produced major discoveries in the science of aesthetic taste. This paper reviews key findings from two complementary approaches: machine learning and large-scale human experiments. We argue that together these approaches represent a fundamental shift in computing aesthetic taste, from measuring preferences and choices to reconstructing the complex, high-dimensional representations that generate them. Using these representations, which we refer to as ‘taste spaces’, researchers can move beyond asking what people like to explaining why they like it, and how aesthetic taste is learned, structured, and transformed across individuals, cultures, and artificial systems. We conclude by discussing how these advances create new opportunities for addressing some of the defining scientific challenges of the coming decades, such as understanding the rich diversity of aesthetic taste across individuals and cultures, and the ways in which artificial intelligence increasingly distorts human taste. © 2026

Title: Motivation for cyberhate among Ukrainian youth
Abstract: While research on cyberhate has focused largely on prevalence and exposure, motivation underlying cyberhate perpetration remains under-researched. This study examines revenge and proactive motivations for cyberhate perpetration among Ukrainian youth during the ongoing war. Guided by the general aggression model, social identity theory, and social cognitive theory, we explored the mediating roles of revenge and proactive motivation in the association between cyberbullying victimization and cyberhate perpetration. Using exploratory structural equation modeling on survey data from 4149 youth aged 10–25, we found that victimization was significantly associated with cyberhate perpetration, partly through revenge motivation. Proactive motivation was related to victimization but was not significantly associated with cyberhate perpetration. Findings highlight the role of revenge motivation in cyberhate behaviors. In this war-affected population, the nonsignificant proactive pathway suggests that cyberhate may differ from forms of online aggression driven by entertainment or social reward. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Optimization of process variables for CO2/CH4 and CO2/N2 binary gas separation using dual-layer hollow fiber mixed-matrix membrane
Abstract: Membrane based carbon dioxide removal from methane, biogas, and process modified streams, such as flue gas recycling, oxy-fuel combustion with air ingress, and industrial exhausts remained a pivotal strategy to curb greenhouse gas emissions and support sustainable energy development. Dual-layer hollow fiber mixed-matrix membranes (DLHFMMMs) have recently garnered substantial attention for CO2 separation, however, optimization of separation variables for such process is still imperative. In this study, design of experiment framework was adopted to perform process optimization of binary gas separation involving CO2/CH4 and CO2/N2 via DLHFMMM. The influences of feed pressure (2–10 bar for CO2/CH4; 5–10 bar for CO2/N2), temperature (30–50 °C), and CO2 feed composition (30–70 vol.% for CO2/CH4; 10–50 vol.% for CO2/N2) on DLHFMMM performance were evaluated. A response surface methodology (RSM) coupled with central composite design (CCD) was utilized to develop predictive models correlating these variables with CO2, CH4 and N2 permeances, along with the corresponding CO2/CH4 and CO2/N2 separation factors. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) identified the most influential factors governing each response, while three-dimensional response surfaces elucidated variable interactions. The optimized conditions for the CO2/CH4 separation (50 °C, 4.420 bar, 70 vol.% CO2) yielded a 22.76 GPU for CO2 permeance together with a CO2/CH4 separation factor of 27.59. For the CO2/N2 binary gas separation, optimal performance (50 °C, 10.000 bar, 50 vol.% CO2) resulted a 14.52 GPU of CO2 permeance and a CO2/N2 separation factor of 46.36. The close agreement between experimental measurements and model predictions confirms the validity of the developed models. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Choi J.-W.; Han G.-M.; Imm J.-Y.
Title: Optimizing melt–stretch properties in yeast protein vegan mozzarella analogues through protein–starch interactions
Abstract: The role of yeast protein (YP) in structuring Mozzarella-type vegan cheese analogues was investigated through its interactions with tapioca starch in composite gel systems. YP exhibited a lower water-holding capacity and smaller particle size (measured in 1%, w/w protein dispersions) than conventional plant proteins, which significantly influenced subsequent gel formation and functionality. Cheese analogues were formulated at varying YP:starch ratios (9:12, 12:9, 15:6, and 18:3), and their physicochemical rheological, microstructural, and functional properties were systematically evaluated. The YP:starch ratio critically governed the network structure, water distribution, lipid organization, and phase stability. At low YP levels, a starch-dominated matrix containing a high proportion of loosely held water lacked a continuous protein network, resulting in limited meltability and stretchability. An intermediate YP:starch ratio (15:6) produced a homogeneous co-continuous protein–starch network with balanced water immobilization and controlled lipid distribution, resulting in the greatest meltability and stretchability. At the highest ratio (18:3), elevated intermolecular β-sheet content was associated with protein aggregation, structural heterogeneity, water over-immobilization, and enlarged lipid domains. These findings demonstrate that the thermo-mechanical functionality of vegan cheese analogues is governed primarily by the structural integration of protein, starch, water, and lipid phases, rather than by protein content alone, providing mechanistic insights for the rational design of high-protein vegan cheese analogues. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Jiang S.; Stadtfeld C.
Title: The social embeddedness of learning: Social network formation and academic achievement in an undergraduate student community
Abstract: Background: Students play an active role in developing their social learning environment and peer relationships. Meanwhile, their academic behaviors are likely to be affected by their integration and individual positions in social networks. Despite the clear importance of social aspects on learning, the mechanisms shaping students’ social networks and the impact of emerging social ties on students’ academic performance remain underexplored. Aims: We investigate (1) the development of undergraduate students’ friendship and co-learning relationships, and (2) the influence of social embeddedness on students’ academic achievement. Sample: The sample consists of first-year students from two large STEM cohorts at a Swiss university: NA=225, NB=625. Methods: With longitudinal network data, we applied stochastic actor-oriented models to simultaneously examine the (co-)evolution of friendship and co-learning networks for each cohort while controlling for other network mechanisms on relationship formation. Furthermore, we implemented network autocorrelation models to examine the influence of social embeddedness on students’ first-year qualification exam GPAs. Results: The results revealed a mutual sustainability of co-learning and friendship ties, which were initially bridged by more generic positive social interactions. Furthermore, we found a significant association between students’ first-year grades and the average grades of their co-learners. This grade interdependency may be a joint outcome of peer selection and peer influence processes. Conclusion: Our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the co-dynamic processes of undergraduate students’ co-learning and friendship networks and highlights the importance of social embeddedness in students’ academic performance. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Zhou Z.; Wu Y.; Fei Y.; Chu J.; Jiang S.; Xu W.; Zheng X.; Wang H.
Title: Hyperuricemia, circulating metabolites, and the risk of cardiometabolic multimorbidity
Abstract: Background The role of hyperuricemia in cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) needs to be further confirmed. We aimed to investigate the impact of hyperuricemia on cardiometabolic multimorbidity, and to explore the metabolic mechanisms. Methods We conducted a prospective cohort study using data from 422,058 participants in the UK Biobank. Cardiometabolic multimorbidity was defined as having two or more cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) identified from linked primary care, hospital, and death registry records. Cox and multistate model was used to examine the role of hyperuricemia in the progression of CMM. Elastic net regression was employed to identify metabolites associated with hyperuricemia, and a weighted hyperuricemia metabolic score was calculated to assess its association with CMM. Results During a median follow-up of 13.65 years, 55,092 developed CMDs, 6484 progressed to CMM, and 2234 died with CMM. Compared with participants without hyperuricemia, those with hyperuricemia had increased risks of any CMDs (HR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.20–1.26, P < 0.001), and CMM (HR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.23–1.42, P < 0.001). Mendelian randomization confirmed causal effects of hyperuricemia on CMDs and CMM. Furthermore, hyperuricemia metabolic score composed of 126 differential metabolites was significantly associated with CMDs (HR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.21–1.27) and CMM (HR = 1.36, 95% CI: 1.28–1.44). In multi-state analyses, the metabolic score was associated with higher risks of transition from health to CMD (HR = 1.25, 95% CI: 1.22–1.28) and from CMD to CMM (HR = 1.15, 95% CI: 1.07–1.22). Conclusions In this large cohort study, hyperuricemia was both observationally and genetically associated with increased risk of cardiometabolic diseases and subsequent progression to cardiometabolic multimorbidity. Hyperuricemia-related metabolic signatures may provide additional insights into the biological processes underlying cardiometabolic disease progression. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: The regulatory roles of the medial septum and hippocampus in spatial memory impairment of PTSD mice
Abstract: This experiment was based on the establishment of an analogue of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in mice, aiming to explore the regulatory effects of the medial septum (MS) and the hippocampus (HIP) on spatial memory impairment in mice, and to establish a theoretical foundation for revealing the pathological basis of PTSD-related spatial memory impairment. The PTSD mouse model was prepared, behavioral testing, FluoroGold (FG) retrograde tracing technique, viral tracing technique, in vivo fiber photometry recording technique, chemogenetic technology and in vivo electrophysiological recording techniques were applied to observe and analyze the changes in spatial memory ability and the central regulatory mechanism. PTSD mice showed heightened anxiety, impaired spatial memory, suppressed Sch-CA1 long-term potentiation, and hyperactivity of MS-CA1 cholinergic neurons; chemogenetic inhibition of this pathway rescued both the behavioral and synaptic plasticity deficits. The regulation of spatial memory impairment in PTSD mice involves MS-resident cholinergic neurons. We found a cholinergic pathway connection between MS and CA1, and this pathway may regulate murine spatial cognition by influencing the synaptic plasticity of Sch-CA1. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Authentic or strategic ESG? Motive attribution, consumer–company identification and purchase intention in retailing
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Against the backdrop of widespread greenwashing skepticism, consumers are increasingly scrutinizing corporate Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) motives rather than simply accepting ESG disclosures at face value, creating a fundamental ethical dilemma in which ESG investment may fail to translate into market returns if corporate actions are attributed to strategic calculation rather than genuine values. Drawing on attribution theory and social identity theory, this study examines how Chinese retail consumers internalize ESG perceptions, through sincere versus strategic motive judgments, into consumer-company identification (CCI), and how this psychological process ultimately drives purchase intention, using a multi-study design in which Study 1 (N = 226) employed a cross-sectional survey of Chinese retail consumers to test the associative pathways and mediation effects among the key variables, while Study 2 (N = 156) employed a single-factor, two-level between-subjects experiment with structural equation modeling (SEM) and 5000-resample bootstrap estimation to examine the proposed direct and indirect effects. Three core findings emerge. First, corporate ESG performance exerts a robust positive effect on purchase intention even in skeptical environments. Second, CCI serves as the critical psychological bridge linking ESG performance to market response. Third, experimental causal evidence reveals that sincere motive attribution is the key trigger for activating CCI, with the indirect effect through identification accounting for 38.3% of the total effect, revealing a “dual-channel structure” in which a direct effect and an indirect, identification-mediated effect coexist. These findings offer actionable implications for ESG communication strategy in China's retail sector and provide a basis for future comparative research in other Asia-Pacific emerging markets. © 2026

Title: Faunal Evidence and the Duration of Occupation: A Statistical Approach to Neanderthal Archaeological Sites
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: The duration of Neanderthal occupations of caves and rock shelters is one of the most debated issues in prehistoric archaeology. Several disciplines, including lithic analysis, micromorphology, zooarchaeology, taphonomy, and spatial archaeology, have proposed criteria to estimate occupation length, but their reliability varies. This study focuses only on indicators derived from faunal assemblages and evaluates their effectiveness through statistical testing. Four features were analysed: number of taxa, hunting spectrum, anthropogenic modifications, and evidence of carnivore activity. These characteristics were applied to a dataset from Late Mousterian sites in Spain and south-eastern France (70–40 ka) that have previously been examined through multidisciplinary approaches. The results indicate that the four features do not provide equally robust signals. Anthropogenic modifications and the number of exploited taxa show the strongest correlation with occupation duration. In contrast, the number of taxa and carnivore activity, when considered alone, are less reliable indicators. Multivariate analyses reveal a clearer structuring of the faunal assemblages. Brief stopping places are consistently distinguished from longer occupations. However, long-term occupations and repeated short-term occupations tend to overlap, largely because of palimpsest effects. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and the limits of faunal criteria. They highlight the need for integrated, high-resolution approaches to reconstruct the duration and intensity of Neanderthal occupations. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Koebner I.J.
Title: Cura: The case for institutionalizing health and well-being in the arts & culture sector
Abstract: A convergent body of evidence from clinical trials, epidemiological cohort studies, mechanistic science and emerging economic analysis demonstrates that arts and cultural engagement is a meaningful determinant of health. Yet the organisational infrastructure of arts and cultural institutions has not kept up with this science. Drawing on the historical example of how education became a permanent institutional vertical in arts and cultural organisations during the twentieth century, this paper argues that the evidence base for arts and health now meets a reasonable threshold for a parallel structural change: the creation within arts and cultural organisations of a permanent, staffed and resourced health and well-being vertical. The argument is normative in its institutional commitments, but deliberately pluralist in form. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Artificial intelligence-based employee selection in tourism and hospitality: Justice, inclusion, and gender differences in resume screening and interviews
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more prevalent in human resource management, its role in tourism and hospitality hiring remains underexplored. This study investigates job applicants’ perceptions of AI in employee selection, focusing on resume screening and interviews. Drawing on fairness heuristic theory and social role theory, we examine how AI affects perceived justice, inclusion, and organizational attractiveness. Four scenario-based experiments and one qualitative study were conducted with job applicants comparing AI-based and human-based selection methods. Results show that human recruiters are generally perceived as more just and inclusive, enhancing organizational attractiveness. However, gender moderates these effects: females favor AI-based resume screening, whereas males are more receptive to AI-based interviews. These findings provide insights for organizations seeking to integrate AI into employee selection while maintaining justice and inclusion. As AI becomes more prevalent in hiring, organizations should prioritize human oversight, ensuring that AI supports rather than replaces human. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Driving police engagement through talent management: Evidence from Abu Dhabi
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between talent management practices and employee engagement, as well as the moderating role of business analytics and the subsequent impact on employee performance within the Abu Dhabi Police. Specifically, the research explores how talent attraction, retention, learning and development, and career management influence employee engagement, which in turn affects job performance. Drawing on social exchange theory, dynamic capability theory, and Aon Hewitt's employee engagement model, a quantitative research design was employed using a structured questionnaire distributed to senior officers across various departments. A total of 383 valid responses were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 3.3.9. The findings reveal that all four dimensions of talent management (talent attraction, talent retention, learning and development, and career management) have significant positive effects on employee engagement. Furthermore, employee engagement strongly and significantly influences employee performance, underscoring its pivotal role in organizational effectiveness. The results of the moderation analysis indicate that business analytics significantly strengthens the relationships between talent attraction, learning and development, and career management and employee engagement, with learning and development and talent attraction showing the strongest moderating effects, whereas the moderating effect on talent retention is statistically insignificant. The model explains 53.8 of the variance in employee engagement, indicating satisfactory predictive power. These findings contribute to the literature by integrating business analytics into the talent management—engagement—performance nexus, particularly within a public sector policing context. Practically, the results highlight the strategic importance of leveraging data-driven and analytics-enabled HRM practices to personalize talent management interventions, enhance perceived fairness, and improve engagement outcomes. Overall, the findings demonstrate that while business analytics enhances most talent management dimensions, its influence is not uniform across all practices, particularly in the case of talent retention. This study provides actionable insights for policymakers and HR leaders seeking to build agile, high-performing, and engaged workforces in dynamic environments. Copyright (c) 2026 The Authors. Authors: Zeng B.; Wider W.; Wu C.; Yang C.; Jiang L.; Tee M.; Wu H.
Title: Identifying and prioritizing key factors influencing electric vehicle fast-charging infrastructure planning in China: A Delphi study
Abstract: The rapid expansion of China's new energy vehicle market has intensified demand for a coordinated, equitable fast-charging infrastructure system. Despite substantial growth, regional disparities, technical incompatibilities, and fragmented governance arrangements continue to constrain the efficiency and long-term sustainability of network deployment. This study systematically identifies and prioritizes the key determinants shaping the planning of fast-charging infrastructure in China. A two-round Delphi process was conducted with 30 experts drawn from government, industry, and academia to establish consensus on critical influencing factors. Anchored in diffusion of innovation and institutional theory, the analysis integrates technological, economic, spatial, social, environmental, and governance dimensions into a coherent evaluative framework. Six principal factors emerged: governance and institutional coordination; economic and financial viability; technological integration and standardization; social equity and user-oriented considerations; spatial and urban planning; and environmental sustainability. Governance and institutional coordination ranked highest in importance, with strong consensus among participants (Kendall's W = 0.696, p < 0.001). The findings underscore the central role of policy coherence, sustainable financial models, and interoperability in accelerating the diffusion of infrastructure and reducing regional inequality. The study advances a theoretically informed prioritization framework to support strategic infrastructure planning in rapidly electrifying economies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Shen X.; Kong J.; Shen X.; Dai F.
Title: Parks as behavioral climate adaptation infrastructure: mechanisms and limits under extreme heat
Abstract: Urban parks are increasingly positioned as critical nature-based solutions for mitigating extreme heat. However, while their physical cooling capacity is well-documented, their role as infrastructure for behavioral climate adaptation remains underexplored. This study examines urban parks as behavioral climate adaptation infrastructure by integrating event-based mobility analysis, park-level adaptation performance assessment, and neighborhood-scale accessibility analysis in the City of Las Vegas. Using anonymized mobility records, extreme heat episodes were identified and linked to changes in visitation intensity, dwell time, and nighttime use. Event-level behavioral responses were summarized using the Park Behavioral Adaptation Index (PBAI), while longer-term park performance was evaluated using the Park Adaptation Performance Score (PACS). Accessibility to higher-performing parks was subsequently assessed in relation to neighborhood social vulnerability. The results reveal three key findings. First, adaptation occurs primarily through temporal reallocation. Second, adaptation performance varies substantially across parks and cannot be explained by park size, morphology, vegetation greenness, or amenity provision alone. Third, access to higher-performing parks is unevenly distributed across the city. Adaptation deficit zones are concentrated in lower-income, renter-dominated, and minority neighborhoods, indicating that opportunities for park-based adaptation are socially unequal. By linking behavioral responses, park performance, and adaptive accessibility within a unified framework, this study shifts attention from the cooling potential of parks to their role in enabling realized adaptation under extreme heat. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Feng J.; Li Y.; Liu Y.
Title: Payroll taxes, firm dynamism, and aggregate productivity
Abstract: This study examines the impact of payroll-tax enforcement on firm dynamism and its implications for aggregate productivity. We exploit China's Social Security Collection Agency Reform, which transferred responsibility for collecting social-insurance contributions from local social-insurance agencies to tax authorities, thereby strengthening enforcement. We show that the reform increased firms’ social-insurance contributions, shifted workers toward informal employment without reducing overall nonagricultural employment, and reduced new firm entry while weakening incumbent firms’ profitability and investment. Overall, the reform reduced measured aggregate productivity in China's registered, above-scale industrial sector by 3.3 percent, with entry into the above-scale industrial sector accounting for about 45 percent of the estimated decline. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Gao R.; Sun Y.; Liu D.; Zhang T.; Bai H.; Wang Z.; Miao Y.; Zhao Y.
Title: Synergistic structure-microenvironment design of polyamide membranes for efficient extraction of lithium from brine
Source title: Journal of Materials Science and Technology
Abstract: Polyamide (PA) membrane has become a promising material for direct lithium extraction from salt lake brine, but it faces the trade-off between permeability and Li+/Mg2+ selectivity. Here, we propose a strategy to resolve this limitation by synergistic regulation of the crosslinked structure of the PA layer and the internal hydrogen-bonding environment. The pre-crosslinking of tannic acid (TA)-modified montmorillonite nanosheets (MMTNS) and polyethyleneimine (PEI) promoted the formation of a PA composite layer with narrow pore size, thereby enhancing Mg2+ rejection. Their synergistic effect also achieves precise regulation of PEI: MMTNS inhibits PEI diffusion in the bulk phase, while TA facilitates its interfacial diffusion. The resulting heterogeneous polymerization dynamics forms a thin and dense PA layer, which enables high Li+/Mg2+ selectivity and ultrafast water transport. In addition, MMTNS and TA construct a rich hydrogen-bonding network that improves the water transport environment and further enhances transport efficiency. The optimized membrane achieves a permeance of 10.08 L m−2 h−1 bar−1 and a Li+/Mg2+ separation selectivity of 49.5, exceeding most currently reported selective Li+ extraction membranes. This work provides insights into the control of the PA layer structure and mass transfer environment, facilitating the design of next-generation selective ion separation membranes. © 2026

Authors: Nguyen L.A.
Title: Approximate minimization of interpretations in fuzzy description logics under the Gödel semantics
Abstract: The problem of minimizing fuzzy interpretations in fuzzy description logics (FDLs) is important both theoretically and practically. For instance, fuzzy or weighted social networks can be modeled as fuzzy interpretations, where individuals represent actors and roles capture interactions. Minimizing such interpretations yields more compact representations, which can significantly improve the efficiency of reasoning and analysis tasks in knowledge-based systems. We present the first algorithm that minimizes a finite fuzzy interpretation while preserving fuzzy concept assertions in FDLs without the Baaz projection operator and the universal role, under the Gödel semantics. The considered class of FDLs ranges from the sublogic of fALC without the union operator and the universal restriction to the FDL that extends fALCreg with inverse roles and nominals. Our algorithm is given in an extended form that supports approximate preservation: it minimizes a finite fuzzy interpretation I while preserving fuzzy concept assertions up to a degree γ∈(0,1]. Its time complexity is O((mlogl+n)logn), where n is the size of the domain of I, m is the number of nonzero instances of atomic roles in I, and l is the number of distinct fuzzy values used in such instances plus 2. Methodologically, our approach fundamentally differs from existing ones, as it avoids quotient constructions traditionally employed for minimizing fuzzy interpretations and fuzzy automata. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Mislin A.
Title: Hidden dissatisfaction after agreement: Post-negotiation perceptual alignment
Abstract: Negotiations continue to have consequences after an agreement or impasse. When parties reach a deal, value is often created only later, as they implement commitments, adapt to uncertainty, or decide whether to negotiate again. This review introduces post-negotiation perceptual alignment, how accurately a negotiator understands the counterpart's post-negotiation experience. Integrating research on subjective value, interpersonal perception, and post-agreement outcomes, I distinguish four states: recognized satisfaction, recognized dissatisfaction, overestimated dissatisfaction, and hidden dissatisfaction. Hidden dissatisfaction is consequential because it creates a false sense of success where one party treats agreement as evidence that the negotiation went well while the counterpart carries forward negative appraisals that remain unrecognized and unaddressed. Recent research suggests tactics that appear successful at agreement can impose unrecognized social and relational costs. I review why misalignment arises, emphasizing how negotiators’ imperfect inferences about counterparts’ experiences can combine with social pressures that discourage dissatisfied parties from speaking up. I conclude by outlining directions for measuring alignment and testing how negotiators can recognize and respond to dissatisfaction after negotiations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Navigating Sustainability of Fisheries in Pulicat Lagoon: An Indicator-Based Multidimensional Assessment
Abstract: Sustainable management of lagoon fisheries requires an integrated assessment of ecological and human dimensions. Pulicat Lagoon, India’s second-largest brackishwater lagoon, supports diverse fisheries and livelihoods but faces threats from anthropogenic activities and environmental degradation. This study applied the modified Rapid Appraisal for Fisheries (RAPFISH) framework to evaluate the sustainability status of Pulicat Lagoon fisheries using a multi-dimensional, indicator-based approach. The ten major fisheries were assessed across five dimensions: ecological, economic, social, technological, and governance based on 34 indicators. Sustainability scores were estimated using multi-dimensional scaling, supported by leverage analysis to identify influential indicators. The overall sustainability score of Pulicat Lagoon fisheries was 47.50%, classifying the system as ‘less sustainable’. Ecological (65.81%) and governance (53.35%) dimensions exhibited relatively better performance, while economic (46.39%), social (43.70%), and technological (28.26%) dimensions remained weak. Penaeid shrimp (53.29%) and crab fisheries (52.92%) showed comparatively higher sustainability than other fisheries. Key drivers influencing sustainability included resilience, fishing income, education, handling and processing practices and research and development support. The findings of this study directly contribute to several key Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), namely SDG 14 (Life Below Water), SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 16 (Strong Institutions). Therefore, these findings highlight the importance of implementing targeted, dimension-specific interventions to strengthen adaptive fisheries management and to ensure the long-term sustainability of fisheries in the Pulicat Lagoon. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Coastal and Estuarine Research Federation 2026.

Title: Precision forensic toxicology: Leveraging Toxicogenomics, multi-omics, and artificial intelligence for next-generation poisoning investigations
Abstract: For much of its history, forensic toxicology was built on a core analytical question: what poison or drug is present, and at what concentration? That question still matters, but modern casework increasingly shows that it is no longer sufficient on its own. The field grew from the nineteenth-century chemical toxicology of Mathieu Orfila and the arsenic-detecting Marsh test into a discipline central to medicolegal death investigation, overdose certification, and exposure reconstruction. Yet contemporary practice must now contend with novel psychoactive substances, highly potent synthetic opioids, complex polysubstance deaths, delayed reporting, postmortem redistribution, matrix degradation, and incomplete toxicological context. These pressures are pushing forensic toxicology beyond simple compound detection toward mechanism-aware, data-rich interpretation. This review develops the idea of precision forensic toxicology as a proposed, forward-looking conceptual framework for that transition rather than a description of established or routinely implemented forensic practice. In this model, classical analytical chemistry remains essential, but it is connected to toxicogenomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics, metabolomics, exposomics, microbiomics, and spatial multi-omics, then integrated through systems toxicology and artificial intelligence. Recent literature shows that toxicogenomics can reveal early molecular perturbations before overt phenotype, that postmortem metabolomics can assist cause-of-death screening, that RNA- and miRNA-based markers may improve postmortem interval estimation, and that machine learning can strengthen high-resolution mass-spectrometry workflows and multi-omics interpretation. At the same time, routine implementation remains constrained by standardization, validation, explainability, privacy governance, and regulatory uncertainty. None of these components is yet part of routine forensic casework; each remains at a research or early-validation stage, and their translation into daily practice will require dedicated feasibility, validation, and regulatory work, which this review discusses explicitly. Taken together, the evidence suggests that the future of poisoning investigation will depend less on any single assay and more on interoperable workflows that connect toxicant detection with biological response, individual susceptibility, and transparent decision support, and that these workflows are intended to complement, not replace, classical toxicological and medicolegal interpretation. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Informal urban regeneration through social capital: The Anousheh Street experience in a developing city
Abstract: While underprivileged neighborhoods are often seen as obstacles to urban development, their regeneration is essential for achieving sustainable urban development. Understanding the factors that influence successful regeneration experiences can guide action in similar neighborhoods. This study examines how the local community drove the informal regeneration of Anousheh Street in Ahvaz, Iran, transforming an underprivileged neighborhood into a vibrant street food hub. This study employed a Straussian Grounded Theory approach based on 24 in-depth interviews, triangulated with secondary socioeconomic data, to explain how the regeneration of Anousheh Street emerged. The findings show that vendor solidarity, rooted in social capital, acts as the central driving mechanism. This solidarity enabled informal creativity in attracting customers, supported by gradual institutional involvement from local authorities. This sequential process drives social, economic, and physical regeneration, evidenced by a 31-fold increase in commercial units and a halving of the local unemployment rate (from 35.27% to 16.81%) between 2011 and 2016. Unlike top-down models, this informal approach preserves cultural authenticity, fostering local identity and economic opportunities. This study develops a novel empirical model demonstrating how urban regeneration in developing cities can be achieved without reliance on large-scale physical investment, instead leveraging social capital and street food-based economies. The model contributes to theory by addressing a key gap in Middle Eastern urban studies and extends the application of Grounded Theory within urban regeneration research. From a practical perspective, this study proposes a context-sensitive yet scalable and transferable model based on three key conditions: vendor solidarity, vendor informal creative practices, and gradual institutional support. While the model demonstrates potential for application in other developing cities, its success depends on local socio-cultural and institutional contexts. These findings provide new policy-relevant insights for advancing inclusive and low-cost urban regeneration in the Global South. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Sun H.; Zhang B.; Zhao Z.; Xing C.; Liu Y.; Huang L.; Liu J.; Shi P.; Wang Q.
Title: Interface-engineered titanium matrix composites with silicon-segregated boundaries for high-temperature strength-ductility synergy
Source title: Journal of Materials Science and Technology
Abstract: High-temperature titanium alloys are approaching intrinsic performance limits, while discontinuous TiB whisker-reinforced composites provide a possible route to higher service temperatures. The central challenge is to improve strength without sacrificing ductility, especially because deformation and fracture are strongly governed by reinforcement interfaces. Here, a hot-extruded TiB/Ti65 composite is developed with ultimate tensile strengths of 1342 MPa at room temperature and 570 MPa at 800 °C. The composite also retains 21.5% ductility at 800 °C, showing a superior strength and ductility combination compared with most reported high-temperature titanium materials. By combining three-dimensional tomography, atomic-resolution microscope, in-situ micromechanical testing, and first-principles calculations, we reveal a Si-segregated TiB/α-Ti interface with enhanced adhesion work. This interface strengthens load transfer to aligned TiB whiskers and promotes pyramidal 〈c+a〉 slip in adjacent α-Ti, thereby improving local deformation compatibility. As a result, interfacial decohesion is suppressed, and ductile fracture is maintained at elevated temperature. These results demonstrate that atomic-scale chemical tailoring of reinforcement interfaces is an effective strategy for overcoming the strength and ductility trade-off in titanium matrix composites designed for extreme environments. © 2026

Title: Corporate social responsibility and socio-economic impacts in the mining sector: A bibliometric review of local community empowerment and sustainable development
Abstract: This study presents a bibliometric analysis of the scholarly literature on corporate social responsibility (CSR) and its socio-economic implications in the mining sector, with a focus on local community empowerment and sustainable development outcomes. Using the Scopus database, a systematic search yielded 217 documents published between 2015 and 2025, which were then refined into 182 articles and reviews through structured inclusion and exclusion criteria. The study covers three main dimensions: (1) the evolution of mining-related CSR publication trends over the period 2015–2025; (2) the identification of dominant countries, institutions, and authors along with evolving collaboration patterns; and (3) thematic clusters that shape the intellectual architecture of the field, specifically how these clusters reflect the tension between corporate interests and stakeholder rights as theorized by Stakeholder Theory. The analysis was conducted using VOSviewer and the Bibliometrix package in R to map publication trends, author productivity, international collaboration networks, and thematic keyword clusters. The findings show a progressive growth in publications, reaching a peak of 37 documents in 2023, reflecting increasing academic and regulatory attention to corporate accountability in the extractive industries. Five thematic clusters were identified: CSR and indigenous peoples, economic sustainability and the resource curse, artisanal mining and local livelihoods, coal mining and occupational health, and a methodological cluster related to data mining in computer science. The United States and Australia lead in publication volume, while Ghana records the highest citation-per-document ratio. Indonesia, while present in the corpus, exhibits limited citation visibility, indicating significant room for increased global research engagement. The study identified critical gaps, including a dearth of longitudinal CSR assessments, limited multinational accountability research, and underrepresentation of Southeast Asian perspectives as urgent research priorities for advancing equitable mining governance. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: Exploring livelihood assets among inland fishing communities: Evidence from the Sungai Pahang, Malaysia
Abstract: The Inland fishing community consisted of Inland fishermen and cage fish farmers. They are among the vulnerable rural groups that require economic assistance. Their dependence on natural resources results in unstable income and increased vulnerability. The vulnerability affects their well-being and livelihoods. Therefore, this study helps by addressing livelihood assets that help minimise vulnerability among the inland fishing community. This paper aims to identify and explore the livelihood assets of inland fishermen and cage fish farmers along the Sungai Pahang. The study employs the Sustainable Livelihood Framework (SLF) to identify five livelihood assets: human, natural, financial, physical, and social assets. A survey was conducted among 521 respondents, including 261 inland fishermen and 260 cage fish farmers, using a structured questionnaire. The study was conducted in five districts along the Sungai Pahang Jerantut, Temerloh, Bera, Maran, and Pekan. The data was then analysed through exploratory factor analysis (EFA) to identify the main dimensions of the five livelihood assets within the inland fishing community groups. The data were also checked with reliability coefficients (Cronbach’s alpha). The findings show that inland fishermen depend heavily on financial assets 79.53% variance and physical assets 76.48% variance, highlighting the importance of access to credit and fishing gear for their livelihoods. In contrast, cage fish farmers mainly rely on social assets, accounting for 77.96% of the variance, and human assets, accounting for 69.67 of % variance. This reflects the cage fish farmers' reliance on relevant government institutions for support, training & skills, health, and experience to sustain cage fish production. Although both community groups share the same river ecosystem, their needs is differ, highlighting the diverse in main livelihood assets within riverine communities. However, both communities identify natural assets as a weak livelihood dimension, reflecting their shared vulnerability. Policy interventions in Malaysia should therefore prioritise river conservation, stricter pollution control, sustainable fishing and aquaculture practices, and community-based environmental awareness programmes. Relevant agencies, including the Department of Environment Malaysia, should collaborate with inland fishing communities to implement integrated, participatory environmental management strategies that enhance livelihood resilience and ensure the long-term sustainability of the Sungai Pahang ecosystem. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: The dynamics of climate change skepticism sharing on social media: Social identity, partisanship, and the impact of negative public opinion cues
Abstract: Social media has facilitated the rapid spread of incorrect information, including climate change skepticism. Drawing on Social Identity Theory, we investigated why individuals adopt skeptical views and disseminate them on social media. Study 1 (N = 316) revealed that Republicans were more likely to endorse climate change skepticism and that those with strong partisan attachments were particularly likely to share these views actively as a manifestation of their social identity. Furthermore, Study 2 (N = 120) designed through the lens of the Spiral of Silence theory revealed that explicit social media cues signaling opposition to climate skepticism (e.g., high number of “dislikes” on posts about climate change skepticism) effectively discouraged climate change skeptics from sharing their skepticism. The findings of the two studies highlight the psychological drivers of climate change skepticism dissemination on social media and demonstrate that explicit cues (e.g., number of “dislikes”) can reduce the spread of climate change skepticism in digital spaces. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Generative AI as a social partner for young adults: Dual pathways to resilience and AI dependence
Abstract: This study examines LLM-based AI chatbots as social interaction partners. It identifies young adults’ support-seeking motivations and models their associations with two interaction processes (Perceived Authenticity and Interaction Intensity) and two psychological outcomes (Resilience and AI Dependence). In Study 1, we developed the Motivation Scale for Generative AI (MS-GAI) through theory-driven item generation and interviews and validated it with a survey of Korean young adults (N = 300). Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported an eight-factor, 40-item structure grounded in four social-support domains and supplemented by context-specific motivations. In Study 2, structural equation modeling showed that Emotional Support and Self-Enhancement were positively associated with both Perceived Authenticity and Interaction Intensity. Objective Advice Seeking was positively associated with Perceived Authenticity, whereas Learning Assistance, Daily Problem-Solving, and Entertainment/Mood Diversion were positively associated with Interaction Intensity. Perceived Authenticity was also positively associated with Interaction Intensity. Both interaction processes were positively related to self-reported Resilience and AI Dependence, with Interaction Intensity showing the stronger association with AI Dependence. These findings identify distinct but overlapping interaction pathways through which support-seeking motivations are associated with adaptive and maladaptive outcomes. The study extends understanding of social support in human–AI interaction by providing a validated motivation measure and showing how shared interaction processes relate to both short-term perceived recovery and dependence. The findings are consistent with the Paradoxes of Technology perspective and highlight the need for emotionally supportive yet balanced design and policy safeguards. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: From hostile feedback to withdrawal: Emotional exhaustion as a barrier to social media misinformation correction
Abstract: User-driven misinformation correction is essential for sustaining the integrity of democratic discourse on social media, yet the emotional costs that discourage engagement remain understudied. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, this study examines how the emotional tone of other users' feedback affects correctors' emotional exhaustion and subsequent willingness to engage in future corrections in a social media environment. In a cross-national experiment (N = 2001) across Austria, Bulgaria, Denmark, and Poland, utilizing a single-factor, four-level between-subjects design, participants corrected misinformation and received feedback varying in valence and arousal. Results show that angry, high-arousal feedback uniquely depletes emotional resources, producing higher exhaustion than civil disapproval or positive feedback. This indicates that critical feedback does not inherently exhaust correctors, but it is the hostile tone, not the negativity itself, that drives depletion. Emotional exhaustion, in turn, predicts avoidance of future corrective engagement. This exhaustion-driven withdrawal is amplified rather than buffered by correction confidence, suggesting that individual motivation alone is insufficient in hostile environments. These findings highlight emotional exhaustion as a key psychological constraint on citizen-led fact-checking and suggest that platform-level moderation targeting hostile comments is critical to protect the emotional resources required for a resilient democratic debate in digital environments. © 2026 The Authors
