Title: Defisherization: The political ecology of small-scale fisheries decline in Indonesia
Abstract: In many coastal areas, the decline of small-scale fisheries is a daily reality for fishers. However, it is still framed as a technical issue, leaving unaddressed the power relations in marine governance that gradually erode fishers' livelihoods. This article develops the concept of defisherization to analyze how conservation-oriented coastal governance and ecological pressures cumulatively erode the livelihoods of small-scale fishers. Based on research in fishing communities along the coast of Buton, Southeast Sulawesi, the study employs observation, in-depth interviews (including a structured household questionnaire), and focus group discussions to examine the dynamics of this transformation. The findings suggest that defisherization occurs through the interplay of four main mechanisms: the narrowing of fishing spaces through permanent conservation zones; ecological pressures that drive household adaptation strategies without fully exiting the fisheries sector; symbolic persistence without adequate material reproduction; and the cumulative interaction between the three that gradually consolidates fisheries as a cultural identity but increasingly marginalizes it as a livelihood. This article offers defisherization as an analytical lens to move beyond explanations that view the decline of small-scale fisheries as an unintended consequence of conservation or environmental crises, demonstrating that environmental governance is vulnerable to undermining the material foundations of livelihoods. In this context, successful ecosystem protection often comes at the cost of compromising the sustainability of small-scale fishers' livelihoods. By offering an analytical lens to understand fisheries decline as a cumulative political-ecological process, this study emphasizes the importance of linking conservation agendas to the sustainable social reproduction of coastal communities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Highly active Ni-Co catalyst on hybrid MWCNT-Graphene nanoplatelet catalysts for ammonia decomposition
Abstract: Ammonia decomposition offers a promising route for on-demand hydrogen production. However, the large-scale use of non-noble metal catalysts is limited by their low activity and poor stability at low temperatures. In this study, a series of monometallic Ni, Co and bimetallic Ni-Co catalysts supported on a hybrid multi-walled carbon nanotube-graphene nanoplatelet were synthesised via impregnation. This study examined how changes in the Ni-Co ratio affect the properties and performance of the catalysts. The catalysts were carefully analysed using XRD, N2 physisorption, CO chemisorption, H2-TPR, H2-TPD, N2-TPD, NH3-TPD, SEM, and TEM. They were then tested for NH3 decomposition at a weight hourly space velocity of 12,000 mL/gcat.h. The results showed that increasing Co content increased the surface area, metal dispersion, and reducibility, while lowering the adsorption and desorption energies for H2, N2, and NH3. The 2.5Ni-7.5Co catalyst had the highest surface area (166.8 m2/g), the best metal dispersion (8.39%), the smallest crystallite size (7.27 nm), and the lowest desorption temperatures and energies for H2, N2, and NH3. It reached 78% NH3 conversion at 500°C and 99% at 550°C, and remained stable for 24h. These findings show that the combination of Ni and Co, along with conductive carbon supports, is important for making efficient, long-lasting, non-noble-metal catalysts for low-temperature NH3 decomposition. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Intellectual overconfidence and susceptibility to anti-science misinformation
Abstract: Anti-science misinformation can undermine trust in science, and understanding who is most susceptible is important for combatting its influence. One relevant trait is Intellectual Humility (IH), associated with greater understanding of science and the reasoning skills required to reject misinformation. Three pre-registered experimental studies (total N = 1604) examined IH and susceptibility to anti-science misinformation in the context of consumer genetic testing. A central subscale of IH – Lack of Intellectual Overconfidence – emerged as the strongest predictor, with intellectually overconfident individuals most susceptible to misinformation, though effect sizes were modest. The final study introduced a warning-label intervention that had a small positive effect on reduced susceptibility to misinformation about genetic testing companies, but only for participants with less intellectual overconfidence, suggesting that those who would benefit most from such interventions may be least likely to do so. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Registered Report Stage I: Signaling green, securing greenbacks: Sustainability claims and venture funding in hospitality & tourism start-ups
Abstract: Tourism's sustainable transition increasingly depends on startups capable of scaling credible innovations. Yet to lead this transformation, they must convince investors that sustainability claims reflect genuine commitment rather than symbolism. This study tests whether, and under what conditions, startups' sustainability communication on X (Twitter) attracts external funding. Integrating signaling and legitimacy theory, we argue that costly, externally validated messages (e.g., stakeholder collaborations or investment-backed actions) enhance pragmatic legitimacy and capital inflow. Analyzing 3869 startups across 94 countries, we link few-shot-classified social-media posts with Crunchbase funding data using a multilevel hurdle model. Title: GRL-DDC: A data-driven paradigm for sustainable governance of online information propagation
Abstract: Online information governance is not merely a problem of predicting diffusion outcomes, but an information-fusion-driven dynamic decision problem that requires balancing credible-information promotion, risk-oriented suppression, and benign-discussion preservation under limited resources. This paper proposes Graph Reinforcement Learning for Dual-Track Diffusion Control (GRL-DDC), a graph reinforcement learning framework for dual-track diffusion control on dynamic graphs. The core innovation of GRL-DDC lies in integrating temporal graph learning, model-based reinforcement learning, constrained intervention, influence maximization/minimization, and misinformation suppression into a unified two-stage framework for online information governance. In the first stage, a temporal graph state-transition predictor fuses observable network structure, node-level semantic states, and user behavioral features to learn short-horizon propagation-state transitions from observational graph snapshots. In the second stage, the trained transition predictor remains fixed and supports a constrained reinforcement learning policy learner that evaluates model-based counterfactual estimates and allocates promotion or suppression actions under explicit budget and action constraints. Experiments on real-world social media data show that GRL-DDC learns an interpretable asymmetric resource-allocation pattern: it prioritizes nodes that contribute to credible or constructive information diffusion while selectively suppressing negative-risk propagation at relatively low cost. These results demonstrate that GRL-DDC provides a feasible data-driven decision-support approach for resource-constrained intervention in dynamic online information diffusion. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: The social implications of classroom seats: replicating and extending previous findings on seating arrangements and peer status
Abstract: This preregistered replication study examined how physical proximity in the classroom is associated with peer perceptions of social status, specifically likeability and popularity. We aimed to replicate and extend the study by van den Berg and Cillessen (2015) using data from 719 students across 33 elementary classrooms (grades 4–6; Mage = 10.27; 51.6% boys). We replicated previous findings by showing that classmates seated closer together concurrently rated each other as more popular and likeable. Furthermore, when given the opportunity to create their own seating arrangements, students placed classmates they found likeable and popular closer to themselves. We extended previous findings by showing that increased proximity between two classmates over time led to an increase in mutual liking, but not perceived popularity. Further, findings did not differ significantly between friends and non-friends. Finally, because extant studies differ in how proximity is measured, we tested an operationalization of proximity in terms of desk clusters. This alternative operationalization produced similar results to its continuous counterpart, highlighting the conceptual and practical value of the current operationalization for future research. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Xu X.; Liu X.; Zhang L.; Wen J.
Title: Inside and out: Exploring how internal and external CSR perceptions influence hospitality employees’ service sabotage
Abstract: Although corporate social responsibility (CSR) has been shown to exert positive effects on hospitality organizations and their stakeholders, the interactive effect of internal CSR (ICSR) and external CSR (ECSR) perceptions on employees’ subsequent service behaviors remains unclear. Drawing on social cognitive theory and cue consistency theory, this study aims to explore how the interaction between ICSR and ECSR perceptions influences employees’ service sabotage. Time-lagged data were collected from 366 hotel employees at two time points and analyzed using hierarchical regression. The results indicate that the ICSR × ECSR interaction has a significant effect on employee service sabotage. Specifically, ECSR perceptions suppress service sabotage only when ICSR perceptions are high. This relationship is mediated by perspective taking. Furthermore, corporate reputational identification strengthens the negative effect of perspective taking on service sabotage. This study offers valuable insights for CSR practices in the hospitality industry and points to promising directions for future research. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Pan Y.; Zhang W.; Guo Z.; Li C.; Yao Y.; Meng X.
Title: Handedness, psychological characteristics, and social adaptation among Chinese college students
Abstract: Handedness may be associated with individual differences in information processing, but its implications for social adaptation remain unclear. This cross-sectional study examined associations among handedness type, openness, cognitive flexibility, multitasking preference, and social adaptation in 3798 Chinese college students. Mixed-handed students reported higher openness (η2 = 0.013), cognitive flexibility (η2 = 0.030), and multitasking preference (η2 = 0.007) than right- and left-handed students, with the largest group difference observed for cognitive flexibility. Left- and right-handed students showed broadly similar scores across these characteristics. Social adaptation was positively associated with openness ( r = 0.20), cognitive flexibility ( r = 0.32), and multitasking preference ( r = 0.23). Mixed-handedness was positively associated with openness ( r = 0.11), cognitive flexibility ( r = 0.17), and multitasking preference ( r = 0.08), whereas its association with social adaptation was weaker ( r = −0.04). Overall, these findings suggest that mixed-handedness is associated with a differentiated pattern of adaptation-relevant psychological characteristics, particularly cognitive flexibility and openness. The results highlight modest but potentially informative individual differences linked to handedness and indicate that these differences are more evident in specific psychological characteristics than in overall social adaptation. Title: Structural Determinants of Household Resilience in Earthquake-Affected Communities: A Case Study from Bawean Island
Abstract: This study examines the socioeconomic impacts of the March 2024 earthquake on household resilience in Bawean Island, East Java, Indonesia. Data for this study were collected through a survey with a snowball sampling technique, with a total of 221 valid respondents from affected regions. Using a household survey across 12 affected villages and partial least squares-structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), the study identifies critical factors contributing to household resilience, namely social, economic, human, and physical capital assets. The findings can be explained in two ways. First, the result confirms social, economic, human, and physical capital as critical resilience determinants. Second, higher household resilience could reduce the impact of natural disasters. This study can be an input for policymakers to strengthen household resilience in disaster-prone areas to support sustainable development goals (SDGs). © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Zhang D.; Huang M.; Jiang X.; Tu N.; Zhao C.; Chen Y.; Chen C.; Huang X.; Zeng R.; Nie X.
Title: The structure and properties of the solid solution of high temperature piezoelectric ceramics: (1-x)Li0.5Bi2.5Nb2O9-xBi3TiNbO9
Abstract: Bismuth layer-structured piezoelectric ceramics have long faced an inherent trade-off between piezoelectric performance and Curie temperature. A novel solid solution (1-x)Li0.5Bi2.5Nb2O9-xBi3TiNbO9 (denoted as (1-x)LBN-xBTN) was designed and fabricated via a conventional solid-state reaction method to achieve a synergistic improvement in both properties. With increasing BTN content, the rotation angle of the oxygen octahedra within the a-b plane increased, resulting in a more pronounced orthorhombic distortion. The Curie temperature rose from 833 °C to 896.3 °C. Furthermore, the refined grain size and increased relative density synergistically enhanced the breakdown electric field. The ferroelectric domains were more fully oriented under high electric fields, significantly improving the remnant polarization and piezoelectric response. The (1-x)LBN-xBTN series of ceramics achieved optimal overall performance when x = 0.5: TC = 861 °C, d33 = 13.0 pC/N, ρdc (at 500 °C) = 2.39 × 107 Ω·cm, demonstrating its promise for high-temperature applications. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Participatory short film production and student well-being: A narrative review from media literacy and sociocultural perspectives
Abstract: In an AI-driven media ecology, short-form video platforms have intensified interest in participatory filmmaking (PFM) as a learner-centered practice in higher education. However, the relationship between student-led short-film production and holistic well-being remains conceptually scattered and methodologically uneven. This narrative review examines how PFM may support student well-being through media literacy and sociocultural learning processes, with particular attention given to the transferability of these mechanisms to Chinese higher education. Peer-reviewed studies published between 2014 and 2025 were searched in Scopus, Web of Science, and CNKI using combinations of “participatory video,” “filmmaking,” “higher education,” and “well-being.” A total of 238 records were screened. Studies were excluded if they focused on non-higher-education settings, addressed media consumption rather than student production, contained no interpretable well-being-related outcomes, or lacked peer-reviewed empirical content. Fifteen studies were retained for full analysis. Data were extracted on context, modality, participants, methods, well-being domains, and pedagogical mechanisms and then coded through a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke and sensitized by media literacy and sociocultural theory. Three recurring mechanisms emerged: reflective authorship, which supports meaning making, critical judgment, and psychological resilience; collaborative scaffolding, which strengthens belonging, shared regulation, and social confidence; and embodied practice, which connects tool-mediated action to attention, physical vitality, and situated learning. However, the evidence base remains small, course bound, and dominated by short-term qualitative designs, with limited work in non-Western settings. This review therefore proposes the participatory filmmaking well-being framework (PFWF) as an empirically anchored synthesis and outlines implications for curriculum design, student support, and future mechanism-testing research in Chinese universities. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Authors: Cheng J.; Zhou S.
Title: Exemption or backfire? The double-edged effect of AI attribution strategy on brand trust in digital content moral crises
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Human-AI collaboration has become central to brand content production, but AI's black-box nature obscures responsibility in digital content moral crises. When such content is perceived as violating widely shared social values, brands increasingly attribute such incidents to AI errors. Prior research has mainly emphasized the responsibility-exemption role of AI attribution strategy, offering limited insight into its moral risks, mixed consequences, and underlying mechanisms. Drawing on the fact-value model, this study conducts five scenario-based experiments to examine how AI attribution strategy affects brand trust in this crisis context. The findings reveal a double-edged effect. At the factual level, this strategy increases consumers' perceived responsibility reduction, thereby producing an exemption effect that supports trust repair. At the value level, it also triggers perceived moral indifference, thereby producing a backfire effect that damages trust. This double-edged effect is moderated by public opinion and consumer traits. High negative electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) dispersion strengthens the perceived responsibility reduction path, whereas low negative eWOM dispersion strengthens the perceived moral indifference path. AI literacy strengthens the exemption effect by helping consumers understand AI-related technical limitations, whereas hostile attribution bias strengthens the backfire effect by leading consumers to question the moral motives behind the brand's technical explanation. This study advances crisis attribution research by examining AI attribution as a proactive brand communication strategy under attribution ambiguity and shows how it can reduce factual blame while raising value-based moral concerns. The findings offer guidance for using AI attribution carefully and reducing ethical communication risks. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Renewable electricity penetration and retail price dynamics: Global evidence on transitional costs of the energy transition
Abstract: The global expansion of renewable energy represents a structural transformation with profound macroeconomic and financial implications. This study investigates the impact of renewable electricity penetration on retail electricity prices using a multi-country panel. The study employs a comprehensive multi-layered empirical framework to address endogeneity, dynamic adjustment, and cross-country structural heterogeneity. The results reveal that renewable penetration is associated with statistically significant short-to medium-term increases in residential electricity prices. However, this effect is nonlinear and conditional on fossil fuel dependence. Once fossil reliance falls below a critical threshold, the marginal price impact weakens substantially. Distributional evidence shows that renewable price effects are amplified in high-price electricity markets. These findings suggest that renewable expansion generates transitional system costs rather than permanent inefficiencies, highlighting the importance of structural conditions in shaping energy transition outcomes and broader economic stability. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Choi Y.; Choi J.; Shin H.; Lee Y.; Kim C.; Kim C.-K.
Title: Dynamic sequential recommendation via lag-aware graph learning
Abstract: Most existing sequential recommenders implicitly assume that feedback is observed immediately after it occurs. This assumption is often violated in production pipelines, where interaction logs can arrive late due to client buffering or downstream feature computation. As a result, the model input at decision time is frequently a censored and temporally misaligned history. In addition, the delay process is rarely stationary in online services, where it can change across users, items, devices, traffic regimes, and time periods. In this paper, we propose DynaLag, a dynamic framework for sequential recommendation via lag-aware dynamic graph learning. DynaLag represents observed user-item interactions as a time-evolving graph and introduces a learnable time-lag adjacency tensor that explicitly routes information across multiple temporal lags. Our method is designed as a lightweight local architecture: dynamic graphs are updated by event-driven insertion into bounded user and item buffers, and inference uses only adaptive local neighborhoods. Experiments on benchmark sequential recommendation datasets under heavy-tailed simulated logging latency show that DynaLag outperforms strong Transformer and graph-based baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/ChoiYoonHyuk/DynaLag. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Genetic inference in social insects: the continued utility of microsatellites in the sociogenomic era
Abstract: Social insects differ from many other biological systems because colonies function as integrated reproductive, ecological, and evolutionary units, often conceptualized as superorganisms. This organization makes genetic inference inherently hierarchical, often requiring genotyping across multiple biological levels: the colony, the population, the individual, and, in some cases, the cellular level. Although whole-genome sequencing and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based approaches are now widely used in population genomics, microsatellites or short tandem repeats remain a useful approach for cost-effective, low-input, and highly replicated genotyping, particularly in the hierarchical sampling designs common in social insect studies. Here, we review the utility and limitations of microsatellites in social insect research using a three-tiered framework spanning colony-, population-, and individual- or cellular-level analyses. Across these scales, microsatellites are especially valuable for colony delimitation, kinship inference, diagnostic screening of known reproductive systems, and low-input genotyping. By comparing the suitability of microsatellites with that of SNP-based and broader genomic approaches across these applications, this review links marker choice to biological scale, sampling design, and inferential goal in studies of social insects. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Zhou Y.; Chen T.; Guo Y.; Hu J.; Hu X.; Ji G.
Title: AC-UKAN: An enhanced U-KAN framework integrating modulated deformable convolution and mixed pooling
Abstract: Accurate medical image segmentation is pivotal for clinical diagnosis. Segmentation targets in medical images differ in appearance, geometric morphology, and contextual organization, which motivates complementary architectural choices rather than a single universal mechanism. We propose AC-UKAN, a depth-specialized extension of U-KAN that assigns modulated deformable convolution (MDConv) to the shallow encoder for input-conditioned geometric sampling, tokenized Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (Tok-KAN) blocks to the low-resolution semantic stages for an alternative nonlinear parameterization, and a mixed pooling module (MPM) to the bottleneck for combined isotropic and anisotropic context aggregation. AC-UKAN was evaluated on the three heterogeneous two-dimensional binary segmentation benchmarks used by U-KAN: BUSI (breast ultrasound), GlaS (gland histopathology), and CVC-ClinicDB (colonoscopic imaging). For a controlled comparison, eight representative segmentation architectures were trained locally under an identical protocol. AC-UKAN achieved an average IoU of 80.78% and DSC of 88.86% with 6.66 M parameters, improving IoU over the U-KAN baseline by up to 4.04 percentage points on the evaluated splits, with its largest gains on BUSI and CVC. Component ablations showed that MDConv and MPM each provided incremental improvements in overlap-based metrics relative to the baseline and to each other's single-module configuration, whereas their combined effect and boundary-distance behavior varied across datasets. Under the official U-KAN protocol, AC-UKAN therefore offers a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off among the evaluated representative architectures, rather than uniform superiority across all three datasets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Epistemological bridges: A systematic review of virtual reality for ethnoscience and culturally responsive learning
Abstract: This research is motivated by the increasing use of VR media in science learning. Therefore, this literature review aims to identify, collect, and analyze scientific publications on the use of VR in the context of culture-based science learning and ethos to answer questions regarding the state, trends, and potential of research, as well as its implications for science learning. Following the PRISMA protocol, the literature published between 2016 and 2025 was searched across four primary databases: Google Scholar, CrossRef, Scopus, and ERIC. Among the initial 535 identified records, 12 peer-reviewed articles met the rigorous inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis. The results demonstrate that VR serves as an epistemological bridge, connecting abstract scientific concepts with concrete, indigenous practices. The analysis reveals that the level of VR immersion significantly affects the research methodology: fully immersive VR is predominantly utilized in small-scale qualitative studies focusing on deep experiential learning, whereas semiimmersive and nonimmersive formats offer broader accessibility for larger-scale classroom implementations. Despite persistent technical hurdles and high implementation costs, the findings indicate that VR consistently enhances students' affective and cognitive domains. It fosters heightened cultural awareness, greater appreciation for traditional knowledge, and a sophisticated understanding of the intersection between science and heritage. However, the review highlights a significant geographic concentration of research and a lack of long-term longitudinal data. This study concludes that while the field is currently a specialized niche, there are substantial opportunities for future research to utilize VR as a medium for integrating diverse knowledge systems into science curricula. These findings suggest that integrating ethnoscience through VR can fundamentally improve the quality and inclusivity of global science education. © 2027, Malque Publishing. All rights reserved.

Title: Hemisphere-aware Graph Convolution and 3D Structural Fusion for multi-modal fMRI brain-disorder classification
Abstract: Multimodal functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a valuable source of information for precisely classifying neurological disorders, which is why it is widely used in the diagnosis of these diseases. However, traditional methods struggle to capture the spatiotemporal dynamics of the brain and single-modality approaches overlook voxel-level structural information. This limits the accuracy of imaging diagnoses of neurological diseases. This study therefore selected resting-state fMRI samples from the Autism Spectrum Disorder (ABIDE) and Parkinson's Disease (PPMI) datasets, proposing the multi-modal half-brain perception framework MSHAGL. This comprises a shared-weight half-brain–whole-brain graph convolutional network (CHW-GCN) and a three-dimensional structure encoder (GBConvNet3D). These are combined with multi-head gated fusion and redundancy suppression loss for joint optimization. Specifically, dynamic maps of the left and right hemispheres and the whole brain are constructed, cross-scale functional connectivity features are extracted, and 3D fMRI volumes are utilized to capture spatial structural patterns. Gating mechanisms achieve dynamic alignment and weighted fusion of temporal-structural features. In classification experiments on the ABIDE and PPMI datasets for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), the results demonstrate that hemispheric perception modelling and multimodal fusion effectively enhance diagnostic sensitivity and robustness while revealing abnormal connectivity and spatial activation patterns related to disease. This provides new tools for supporting clinical decisions about brain diseases and discovering imaging biomarkers. Our code at https://github.com/Aurora-s-02/MSHAGL. © 2026

Title: Text-driven causal mapping of PET/rPET circularity in Australia: A dynamic factor–network analysis
Abstract: PET circularity is often evaluated by recovery volumes, although performance ultimately depends on whether recovered material can be converted into quality-assured outputs and absorbed by viable end markets. Yet the mechanisms connecting policy, markets, technology, and stakeholder behavior remain dispersed across heterogeneous evidence. We developed a source-attributed, time-stamped causal-network approach using 750 Australian government, industry and NGO, corporate, and media documents published during 2010–2025. Causal extraction, semantic normalization, sentiment assignment, and graph construction yielded 2794 factor nodes and 1588 unique causal edges. The network was strongly externalized: policy, market, and social factors were more numerous and highly connected than internal technical and operational factors. Persistent barriers combined cost and price volatility, inconsistent recyclate quality, infrastructure gaps, and weak policy implementation. Positive mechanisms clustered around standards and measurement, design for recyclability, operational capacity, and end-market development; their circular value depended on retained material quality and the end use reached. Source attribution revealed systematic framing differences, with media coverage concentrating negative implementation narratives. Temporal and regional analyses indicated a shift from limited attention to rapid expansion and subsequent consolidation, alongside national structural hubs and differentiated state pathways. A full-text academic shadow corpus preserved the broad problem domains but changed their hierarchy: academic evidence foregrounded material and processing mechanisms, whereas the primary corpus foregrounded institutional coordination and market implementation. The contribution is therefore not a universal ranking of Australian interventions, but an auditable framework for identifying how technical feasibility becomes, or fails to become, operational circularity under different institutional conditions. © 2026 The Authors
